parts.text: Now I have a clear picture of the tech stack. Let me explain it concisely.

**Tech Stack:**

| Layer | Technology |
|-------|-----------|
| **Framework** | Next.js 16 (with Turbopack, App Router) |
| **Language** | TypeScript 5 (strict mode) |
| **UI** | React 19, Tailwind CSS 4 |
| **Database/Auth** | Supabase (PostgreSQL + auth) |
| **Payments** | Razorpay |
| **Linting** | ESLint 9 |
| **Deployment** | Vercel (vercel.json present) |

**Why this stack?**

- **Next.js 16 + React 19** — Gives SSR/SSG/ISR, file-based App Router, and the latest React features (RSC, Server Components, streaming) for a fast, SEO-friendly multi-role platform.
- **Supabase** — Provides auth, PostgreSQL DB, and real-time subscriptions out of the box. No backend to manage — perfect for a startup with consumer, farmer, rider, moderator, and admin roles (5 separate session managers in `src/lib/`).
- **Tailwind CSS 4** — Utility-first, ships zero CSS by default, pairs well with Next.js for rapid UI iteration.
- **Razorpay** — Standard Indian payment gateway, needed for the marketplace payment flow.
- **TypeScript strict** — Catches bugs early in a multi-role codebase with complex business logic (pricing, delivery fees, demand-supply, etc.).
- **Vercel** — Native Next.js deployment with edge functions, serverless, and CI/CD.

The architecture is a **monorepo-less full-stack Next.js app** with a thick `lib/` layer (31 modules) handling all business logic — no separate backend. Roles are split by route groups (`/farmer`, `/consumer`, `/rider`, `/moderator`, `/admin`) each with their own auth context and components.
